title: Photosynthesis: how plants make food from light
subject: Biology
summary: Plants capture sunlight in chloroplasts and turn water and carbon dioxide into glucose and oxygen.

scenes.heading: A leaf is a solar-powered kitchen
scenes.narration: Every green leaf is a tiny kitchen. Its power source is sunlight, and its job is to cook sugar the plant can use as food.

scenes.heading: The ingredients
scenes.narration: The recipe needs three things. Water pulled up from the roots, carbon dioxide breathed in from the air, and light from the sun.

deeper.heading: Water comes up from the roots
deeper.narration: Roots soak up water from the soil. Thin tubes called xylem carry it all the way up the stem into the leaf.

deeper.heading: Carbon dioxide comes in through pores
deeper.narration: The underside of a leaf has tiny pores called stomata. They open to let carbon dioxide drift in from the air.

deeper.heading: Light is the energy, not an ingredient you can hold
deeper.narration: Sunlight is not mixed in like flour. It is the energy that powers the reaction, like heat from a stove.

checkpoint.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three things the leaf's recipe needs?
checkpoint.hint: Think about what the plant takes in, not what it gives out.
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Yes: oxygen is something the plant releases, not an ingredient.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: That one is an ingredient. Listen again to the three things the recipe needs.
checkpoint.explanation: The recipe is water, carbon dioxide and light. Oxygen is made, not used.

scenes.heading: Chlorophyll catches the light
scenes.narration: Inside the leaf are chloroplasts, packed with a green pigment called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light, and reflects green, which is why leaves look green.

deeper.heading: Light is a mix of colours
deeper.narration: White sunlight is really a mix of colours, from red to violet. Different pigments grab different colours.

deeper.heading: Chlorophyll is picky
deeper.narration: Chlorophyll grabs red and blue light strongly but barely uses green. The green bounces off and reaches your eyes.

deeper.heading: Captured light becomes chemical energy
deeper.narration: The energy chlorophyll captures is stored in carrier molecules, ready to build sugar in the next step.

checkpoint.q: Why do most leaves look green?
checkpoint.hint: What happens to the colours chlorophyll does NOT absorb?
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Right: green light bounces off, so that's the colour we see.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: Close, but think about which colours chlorophyll keeps and which it sends back.
checkpoint.explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green, so green reaches your eyes.

scenes.heading: The recipe
scenes.narration: Put it together and you get the photosynthesis equation. Six carbon dioxide plus six water, powered by light, make one glucose and six oxygen.

deeper.heading: Read the left side
deeper.narration: On the left are the inputs: six molecules of carbon dioxide and six of water.

deeper.heading: Read the right side
deeper.narration: On the right are the outputs: one molecule of glucose, the sugar, and six of oxygen gas.

deeper.heading: Atoms are conserved
deeper.narration: Count the atoms. Six carbons, twelve hydrogens and eighteen oxygens on each side. Nothing is lost, just rearranged.

checkpoint.q: Photosynthesis makes glucose and what else?
checkpoint.hint: It's the gas you breathe in.
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Yes: six oxygen molecules come out with one glucose.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: That one goes in, not out. Look at the right side of the equation.
checkpoint.explanation: 6 CO2 + 6 H2O, powered by light, make 1 glucose + 6 O2.

scenes.heading: Why it matters to you
scenes.narration: The glucose feeds the plant and, through food chains, feeds you. The oxygen is released into the air you breathe.

quiz.q: Which gas do plants take in for photosynthesis?

title: Photosynthesis in 60 seconds (equation focus)
subject: Biology
summary: A fast walkthrough of the photosynthesis equation and its two stages.

scenes.heading: Two stages
scenes.narration: Photosynthesis happens in two stages: the light reactions and the Calvin cycle.

scenes.heading: Light reactions
scenes.narration: Light splits water, releasing oxygen and charging up energy carriers called ATP and NADPH.

checkpoint.q: In the light reactions, what gets split?
checkpoint.hint: The oxygen we breathe comes from it.
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Yes: light splits water, which releases oxygen.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Which molecule gives up its oxygen in this stage?
checkpoint.explanation: Light splits water, releasing oxygen and charging ATP and NADPH.

scenes.heading: Calvin cycle
scenes.narration: The Calvin cycle spends that energy to fix carbon dioxide into glucose.

checkpoint.q: What does the Calvin cycle turn into glucose?
checkpoint.hint: It's the gas plants take in from the air.
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Right: it fixes carbon dioxide into glucose.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: That isn't what gets 'fixed'. Think about where the carbon in glucose comes from.
checkpoint.explanation: The Calvin cycle uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into glucose.

scenes.heading: The equation
scenes.narration: Overall: six CO2 plus six H2O gives glucose plus six O2.

quiz.q: Where does the oxygen released in photosynthesis come from?

title: Newton's three laws of motion
subject: Physics
summary: Inertia, F = ma, and action-reaction, explained with a skateboard.

scenes.heading: Meet the skateboard
scenes.narration: We'll use one skateboard to understand all three of Newton's laws.

scenes.heading: Law 1: Inertia
scenes.narration: An object keeps doing what it is doing unless a force acts on it. A still skateboard stays still. A rolling one keeps rolling until friction slows it.

deeper.heading: Inertia means resisting change
deeper.narration: Inertia is an object's tendency to resist changes in motion. It is not a force, it is a property.

deeper.heading: Why things seem to stop by themselves
deeper.narration: On Earth, friction and air resistance are invisible forces that slow things down. In space, a pushed object would glide forever.

deeper.heading: Seatbelts are inertia in action
deeper.narration: When a car brakes, your body keeps moving forward. The seatbelt supplies the force that stops you.

checkpoint.q: A skateboard is rolling on a smooth path. Why does it eventually stop?
options: Objects always slow down by themselves
checkpoint.hint: The first law says it keeps rolling unless something acts on it. What acts on it?
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Exactly: friction is the force that slows it.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: The first law says motion doesn't just run out. Which force did the scene mention?
checkpoint.explanation: An object keeps moving unless a force acts on it; here, friction is that force.

scenes.heading: Law 2: F = ma
scenes.narration: Force equals mass times acceleration. Push an empty skateboard and it zooms. Push one carrying your friend just as hard and it barely speeds up.

visual.note: more mass → less acceleration for the same push

deeper.heading: What each letter means
deeper.narration: F is the net force in newtons. m is mass in kilograms. a is acceleration in metres per second squared.

deeper.heading: Try a number
deeper.narration: A 2 kilogram board pushed with 10 newtons accelerates at 5 metres per second squared. Ten divided by two is five.

deeper.heading: Double the mass
deeper.narration: Put a 2 kilogram backpack on it, so 4 kilograms total. The same push now gives only 2.5. Double the mass, half the acceleration.

checkpoint.q: You push two skateboards equally hard. One carries a friend. Which speeds up less?
checkpoint.hint: More mass, same force: what happens to acceleration?
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Yes: more mass means less acceleration for the same force.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: Think about F = ma. If F stays the same and m goes up, what happens to a?
checkpoint.explanation: F = ma, so with the same force, a bigger mass gets a smaller acceleration.

scenes.heading: Law 3: Action and reaction
scenes.narration: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Push off a wall on your skateboard and the wall pushes you back just as hard.

checkpoint.q: You push off a wall on a skateboard. What does the wall do?
options: Pushes you back just as hard
checkpoint.hint: Every action has an equal and opposite...
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Right: equal and opposite reaction.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: Walls do push back. How hard, according to the third law?
checkpoint.explanation: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.

quiz.q: Same push, twice the mass. What happens to acceleration?
A rolling ball on a perfectly frictionless surface will…

title: Causes of the French Revolution
subject: History
summary: Debt, inequality and new ideas pushed France to revolution in 1789.

scenes.heading: France, 1789
scenes.narration: In 1789 France was rich in palaces but broke in its treasury. Bread prices were soaring and people were hungry.

scenes.heading: Three Estates
scenes.narration: Society was split into three estates. Clergy and nobles were a tiny minority but paid almost no taxes. The Third Estate, everyone else, paid for nearly everything.

deeper.heading: Who was in each estate
deeper.narration: The First Estate was the clergy. The Second was the nobility. The Third was everyone else, from poor peasants to wealthy lawyers.

deeper.heading: Why it felt unfair
deeper.narration: Each estate got one vote, so the two privileged estates could always outvote the Third, even though it was 98 percent of the people.

deeper.heading: The breaking point
deeper.narration: In June 1789 the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly and swore the Tennis Court Oath, refusing to leave until France had a constitution.

checkpoint.q: Which group paid for nearly everything?
checkpoint.hint: It was the biggest group: everyone else.
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Yes: the Third Estate carried the tax burden.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: That group was a small minority that paid almost no taxes.
checkpoint.explanation: Clergy and nobles paid almost no tax; the Third Estate paid for nearly everything.

scenes.heading: A kingdom in debt
scenes.narration: Wars, including helping the Americans win independence, left France deeply in debt. King Louis the Sixteenth tried to raise taxes, which made everything worse.

checkpoint.q: What made France's debt worse?
checkpoint.hint: Think about what the scene said cost so much money.
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Right: wars left France deeply in debt.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Which costly events did the scene name?
checkpoint.explanation: Wars, including helping the Americans win independence, left France deeply in debt.

scenes.heading: Dangerous new ideas
scenes.narration: Enlightenment thinkers like Rousseau and Voltaire argued that power should come from the people and that all citizens deserve equal rights.

scenes.heading: The spark
scenes.narration: On the fourteenth of July 1789, crowds stormed the Bastille prison. The revolution had begun.

quiz.q: Which group paid most of the taxes?
Which event on 14 July 1789 marks the start of the revolution?

title: Mitosis: how one cell becomes two
subject: Biology
summary: The four phases of mitosis, remembered with PMAT.

scenes.heading: Why cells divide
scenes.narration: You grow and heal because your cells copy themselves. Mitosis makes two identical cells from one.

scenes.heading: Prophase
scenes.narration: Chromosomes coil up and become visible, and the nuclear envelope starts to break down.

scenes.heading: Metaphase
scenes.narration: Chromosomes line up in the middle of the cell, like students lining up in a hallway.

checkpoint.q: What happens in metaphase?
options: Chromosomes line up in the middle
checkpoint.hint: Remember the hallway comparison.
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Yes: they line up in the middle, like students in a hallway.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: That's a different phase. What did the hallway picture show?
checkpoint.explanation: In metaphase chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell.

scenes.heading: Anaphase
scenes.narration: Spindle fibres pull the sister chromatids apart to opposite ends of the cell.

checkpoint.q: In anaphase, what pulls the sister chromatids apart?
checkpoint.hint: They stretch across the cell like ropes.
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Right: spindle fibres pull them to opposite ends.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Which structures act like ropes in this phase?
checkpoint.explanation: Spindle fibres pull the sister chromatids to opposite ends of the cell.

scenes.heading: Telophase
scenes.narration: New nuclei form around each set, and the cell pinches in two. Remember it as PMAT.

quiz.q: In which phase do chromosomes line up in the middle?

title: The Pythagorean theorem
subject: Math
summary: Why a² + b² = c² works for every right triangle, with a ladder example.

scenes.heading: A ladder problem
scenes.narration: A ladder leans against a wall. The foot is 3 metres out, and it reaches 4 metres up. How long is the ladder?

visual.caption: 3 m out, 4 m up, how long?

scenes.heading: Right triangles
scenes.narration: The wall, ground and ladder make a right triangle. The longest side, opposite the right angle, is the hypotenuse.

checkpoint.q: In a right triangle, which side is the hypotenuse?
options: The side next to the right angle
The longest side, opposite the right angle
checkpoint.hint: Look across from the square corner.
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Yes: it's the longest side, opposite the right angle.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Where is it compared with the right angle?
checkpoint.explanation: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is always the longest side.

scenes.heading: The theorem
scenes.narration: Square the two legs and add them. That equals the square of the hypotenuse.

checkpoint.q: A right triangle has legs of 6 and 8. What is the hypotenuse?
checkpoint.hint: Square each leg, add, then take the square root.
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Yes: 36 + 64 = 100, and the square root of 100 is 10.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: Check the last step: did you take the square root of the sum?

scenes.heading: Solve it
scenes.narration: Three squared is nine, four squared is sixteen. Nine plus sixteen is twenty-five, and the square root of twenty-five is five. The ladder is 5 metres.

quiz.q: A right triangle has legs 6 and 8. What is the hypotenuse?

title: Supply and demand
subject: Economics
summary: How prices are set where buyers and sellers meet, using concert tickets.

scenes.heading: Concert tickets
scenes.narration: Your favourite artist announces one show. Thousands want tickets but there are only so many seats.

scenes.heading: Demand
scenes.narration: Demand is how much people want to buy at each price. When price goes up, people buy less.

checkpoint.q: Ticket prices go up. What usually happens to how many people want to buy?
checkpoint.hint: Think about how you react when something gets pricier.
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Right: higher price, lower quantity demanded.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. What did the scene say people do when price rises?
checkpoint.explanation: Demand: when price goes up, people buy less.

scenes.heading: Supply
scenes.narration: Supply is how much sellers offer at each price. Higher prices make sellers want to sell more.

scenes.heading: Equilibrium
scenes.narration: The market price settles where the amount people want to buy equals the amount sellers offer. That is equilibrium.

checkpoint.q: What is equilibrium?
options: Where buyers want exactly what sellers offer
checkpoint.hint: It's where the two amounts meet.
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Yes: the price where buyers' and sellers' amounts match.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Equilibrium is about two amounts being equal. Which two?
checkpoint.explanation: Equilibrium is where the amount people want to buy equals the amount sellers offer.

quiz.q: If price rises, quantity demanded usually…

scenes.heading: One drop, many journeys
scenes.narration: The water you drink today might once have been in a dinosaur, a glacier or a cloud.

scenes.heading: Evaporation
scenes.narration: The sun heats oceans and lakes, turning liquid water into invisible water vapour.

checkpoint.q: What turns liquid water into water vapour?
checkpoint.hint: Evaporation needs energy. Where does it come from?
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Yes: the sun heats the water and it evaporates.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Which one adds energy to the water?
checkpoint.explanation: The sun heats oceans and lakes, turning liquid water into vapour.

scenes.heading: Condensation
scenes.narration: High up it is cold, so vapour cools and condenses into tiny droplets that form clouds.

checkpoint.q: Why does water vapour form clouds high up?
checkpoint.hint: What is the air like high up?
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Right: it cools and condenses into droplets.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: Think about temperature high in the sky.
checkpoint.explanation: High up it is cold, so vapour cools and condenses into tiny droplets.

scenes.heading: Precipitation and collection
scenes.narration: Droplets merge until they are heavy enough to fall as rain or snow, collecting in rivers and oceans to start again.

title: Ionic vs covalent bonds
subject: Chemistry
summary: Atoms either give away electrons (ionic) or share them (covalent).

scenes.heading: Atoms want full shells
scenes.narration: Atoms are most stable with a full outer shell of electrons. Bonds are how they get there.

scenes.heading: Ionic: give and take
scenes.narration: In table salt, sodium gives one electron to chlorine. Now one is positive, one negative, and opposites attract.

checkpoint.q: In table salt, what does sodium do?
checkpoint.hint: Ionic bonds are about giving and taking.
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Yes: sodium gives one electron, so it becomes positive.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. In an ionic bond, is the electron shared or handed over?
checkpoint.explanation: Sodium gives one electron to chlorine; the opposite charges attract.

scenes.heading: Covalent: sharing
scenes.narration: In water, oxygen shares electrons with two hydrogens. Nobody gives anything away, they share.

scenes.heading: Quick test
scenes.narration: Metal plus non-metal usually means ionic. Two non-metals usually means covalent.

checkpoint.q: Two non-metals usually form which kind of bond?
checkpoint.hint: Think about water: oxygen and hydrogen.
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Right: two non-metals usually share electrons, which is covalent.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. What kind of bond did water have?
checkpoint.explanation: Metal + non-metal is usually ionic; two non-metals usually covalent.

title: The Industrial Revolution
subject: History
summary: How steam power and factories reshaped work and cities from the 1760s.

scenes.heading: Before machines
scenes.narration: In 1750 most people farmed and made goods by hand at home.

scenes.heading: Steam changes everything
scenes.narration: James Watt's improved steam engine could power machines anywhere, not just next to rivers.

checkpoint.q: Why was Watt's improved steam engine such a big deal?
options: It was the first machine ever
Machines could run anywhere, not just by rivers
checkpoint.hint: Before it, where did factories have to be built?
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Yes: factories no longer needed to sit next to rivers.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Think about where machines could be used before and after.
checkpoint.explanation: Steam could power machines anywhere, not only next to rivers.

scenes.heading: Cities explode
scenes.narration: People moved to cities for factory jobs. Cities grew fast, often crowded and polluted.

checkpoint.q: Why did cities grow so fast?
options: People moved there for factory jobs
checkpoint.hint: Where were the new jobs?
checkpoint.feedback_correct: Right: people followed the factory jobs.
checkpoint.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. What drew people to cities in the scene?
checkpoint.explanation: People moved to cities for factory jobs, so cities grew fast.

scenes.heading: Winners and losers
scenes.narration: Goods got cheaper and new wealth was created, but workers, including children, faced long hours and dangerous conditions.

quiz.q: Which invention let factories be built away from rivers?
